Request Info
The Doctoral Program in Applied Physics & Nanotechnology prepares students to enter the scientific and engineering workforce as scientists engaged in research and development in processing of semiconductors, novel materials research, solid state devices and batteries, non-crystalline and soft materials, fluids and elastic materials, micro and nanofabrication and lithographic techniques, and related topics.

At a Glance
Comprehensive, In-Depth Doctoral Preparation: Master advanced scientific concepts over 10 to 12 semesters. A robust 53-credit workload ensures a deep, comprehensive mastery of applied physics and nanotechnology.
Pioneering Breakthroughs in Materials & Nanoscience: Engage in breakthrough theoretical work—from dynamical systems to electronic structure calculations—and conduct experimental research in soft materials, superconductors, nanoscale magnetism, and high-energy-density materials.
High-Demand Expertise at the Intersection of Physics & Tech: Transform deep technical expertise and rigorous quantitative skills into high-impact careers. Graduates stand out to top employers in defense, robotics, renewable power, semiconductors, biotech, and advanced materials processing.
Program Details
Applied Physics and Nanotechnology are interdisciplinary fields built around the application of leading-edge physical principles and concepts. Knowledge of the relationship between the structure of materials at the atomic scale and their macroscopic properties provides the foundation for the development of new classes of materials and devices with tailor-made properties, and forms the basis for paradigm shifting technological advances.
This program is open to students from any of the sciences, mathematics, and engineering disciplines, and is designed to teach students from diverse backgrounds the fundamentals of applied physics and nanotechnology. The program is built around a hands-on,cutting-edge curriculum taught by leading scientists and experienced instructors specializing in nanotechnology and materials physics. Students will be mentored by active scientists and researchers and encouraged to make full use of state-of-the-art facilities. A key goal of the program is to provide students with ample opportunity to learn the practical aspects of cutting edge experimental, nanofabrication, microfabrication, and characterization methods, leading to a skill-set that allows them to transition from academia to industry. The course work is designed around the needs of students from varied backgrounds and will provide the required conceptual pre-requisites.
Selection Criteria
Students with or about to earn bachelor’s degrees in any of the sciences, in mathematics, or in engineering and other technical disciplines will be eligible for the doctoral program. Selection criteria for the program includes GPA and GRE scores, professional experience, and recommendations. Note that GRE scores may be waived on a case-by-case basis. Students will develop a course schedule in consultation with a member of the Physics faculty and the program director, who will serve as their advisor.
Play Video
Curriculum
Candidates for a PhD must complete at least 53 credit hours of graduate course work,pass the comprehensive examination, and write and successfully defend a dissertation based on original research (in addition to other departmental and University requirements.) For successful completion of the degree, the cumulative GPA must be at least 3.0. If a student gets a ‘C’ (or lower grade) in a course he/she may be allowed - at the discretion of the program director - to retake that course to improve the grade to at least ‘B’. Two ‘C’ grades will lead to automatic expulsion of the student from the program. Courses will be selected from an approved list of courses and must be approved by the program director who has final say in these matters.
The comprehensive exam, which is usually taken in the fourth semester, is an oral presentation based on a topic selected in mutual consultation with the program director and the student’s research mentor (if applicable.) The exam committee will ask questions based on the entirety of the student’s prior course work in the program as well as questions based on their presentation.
As the program is designed around the educational needs of a diverse group of students from different backgrounds such as biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics, and allied technical disciplines, all students will be required to take at least six “Core Courses” as identified in the list of approved core courses.
We may allow course substitutions on a case-by-case basis and at the discretion of the program director. Students will receive extensive guidance from their academic advisor and program director to tailor a course of study consistent with student interests and program requirements.
Students will be expected in their third semester (if not earlier) to select a faculty member from the Physics Department who will serve as their dissertation director. Together, they will identify an original research problem with the student embarking on independent research no later than after completing 30 credit hours of coursework.
